title: A dynamic stimulus distribution methodology for efficient large-scale pairwise relational data collection
author: Chuyin, Lipeng, et al.

steps.title: Prepare and upload frequency CSV
steps.instruction: Create a melted‑matrix CSV on your computer (use R melt() on a matrix). The first column must contain the relative file path of video 1, the second column the path of video 2, and the third column the number of times that pair has been shown. If you want to study order effects, record (stimulus A, stimulus B) and (stimulus B, stimulus A) as separate rows. Ensure the file contains **no quotation marks** and **delete the empty row at the end**. Go to https://gist.github.com, log in, click “Create a new gist”, paste the CSV content, give it a filename (e.g., frequency.csv), select **Create public gist**, and save.

substeps.instruction: Generate melted matrix CSV (columns: video1 path, video2 path, count).
Remove any quotation marks from the file.
Delete the final empty row.
Create a new public gist on GitHub Gist and upload the CSV.

steps.title: Locate Gist ID and set up PsychoPy code component
steps.instruction: After the gist is created, copy the two strings that appear after “gist.github.com/” in the browser URL – the first is your GitHub username, the second is the Gist ID (e.g., 2f7f88e810b711e4f3bf21a13727e28c). Open your experiment in PsychoPy (online version on Pavlovia), add a **Code** component from the “Custom” toolbox, place it in the first routine, set the code type to **JavaScript**, and ensure the code is placed under **Begin experiment**. All subsequent JavaScript snippets will go into this component.

substeps.instruction: Copy username and Gist ID from the gist URL.
In PsychoPy, add a Code component (Custom → Code).
Set the component to run in “Begin experiment” and language to JavaScript.

steps.title: Fetch and process frequency data

substeps.instruction: Replace <GIST_ID> with your actual Gist ID.
Replace 'frequency.csv' if your file has a different name.
Replace the keys array if your column names differ.
The code fetches the gist, reads the CSV as text, splits it into rows, builds a numeric array, converts it to an object array, shuffles entries with equal frequency, and sorts by the count value.

steps.title: Generate stimulus list for participant

substeps.instruction: Identify the minimum count (`lowest1`).
Select one pair with that count as the start stimulus.
Initialize `sequence` with the two video paths of the start pair.
Add additional stimuli to `sequence` based on the sorted `frequency` array according to your experimental constraints.

steps.title: Create GitHub personal access token
steps.instruction: In GitHub, go to **Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic)**. Click **Generate new token**, give it a name, set an expiration date, tick the **gist** scope, and click **Generate token**. Copy the generated token (e.g., `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`).

substeps.instruction: Navigate to Developer settings → Personal access tokens (classic).
Generate a new token, enable the “gist” scope, and copy the token.

steps.title: Update frequency matrix and overwrite Gist

substeps.instruction: Re‑fetch the latest frequency data to obtain `currentfrequency`.
Loop through `sequence` (from index 1 to `sequence.length‑49`) and increment the appropriate `value` entries (ignore the `else if` block if order matters).
Create `newfrequency` array, prepend header row with your column names, push each row’s values, join rows with commas and newlines to form `filecontent`.
Patch the gist via AJAX using your personal access token, gist ID, and file name.
